paper_title: Attributing Response to Context A Jensen-Shannon Divergence Driven   Mechanistic Study of Context Attribution in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
caption: Computational efficiency comparison between our ARC-JSD and Contextcite (n=256 calls) across all datasets and RAG models. Each bar represents the average seconds per sample for ARC-JSD and Contextcite with different RAG models and datasets.

model_annotations.English: The bar chart titled "Computational Efficiency: ARC-JSD vs. Contextcite" presents a comparison of average processing time (in seconds per sample) for two context attribution methods—ARC-JSD and Contextcite—across four different RAG models (Qwen2-1.5B-IT, Qwen2-7B-IT, Gemma2-2B-IT, Gemma2-9B-IT) and three datasets (TyDi QA, Hotpot QA, MuSiQue), based on 256 model calls per configuration. The horizontal axis lists the models in the order specified, while the vertical axis represents "Seconds/Sample" on a linear scale ranging from 0 to 80, with major tick marks at 20, 40, 60, and 80. For each model, there are six grouped bars corresponding to the two methods and three datasets, differentiated by color: dark blue for ARC-JSD - TyDi QA, orange for Contextcite - TyDi QA, light blue for ARC-JSD - Hotpot QA, peach for Contextcite - Hotpot QA, light gray for ARC-JSD - MuSiQue, and tan for Contextcite - MuSiQue. Across all models, Contextcite consistently requires more computational time than ARC-JSD, with particularly large differences in the MuSiQue dataset (e.g., for Gemma2-9B-IT, Contextcite-MuSiQue reaches ~85 seconds/sample whereas ARC-JSD-MuSiQue is around 30 seconds/sample). The shortest bars (indicating fastest processing) are ARC-JSD on TyDi QA for all models (ranging from ~1.5 to ~5 seconds/sample), while the tallest bars are Contextcite on MuSiQue, especially for Gemma2-9B-IT, which exceeds 80 seconds/sample. Bars are arranged in groups by model, with within-group ordering consistent with the legend (ARC-JSD first, then Contextcite, for each dataset), and no visual emphasis such as outlines or annotations is applied to any bar.
model_annotations.German: The bar chart titled "Computational Efficiency: ARC-JSD vs. Contextcite" compares the average processing time in seconds per sample for two methods—ARC-JSD and Contextcite—across four different RAG models (Qwen2-1.5B-IT, Qwen2-7B-IT, Gemma2-2B-IT, Gemma2-9B-IT) and three datasets (TyDi QA, Hotpot QA, MuSiQue). The horizontal axis lists the models in the order presented, while the vertical axis, labeled "Seconds/Sample," ranges from 0 to 80 with major gridlines at intervals of 20. Each group of bars corresponds to a model, with three pairs of bars per group: one pair for each dataset. Within each dataset group, the first bar (darker blue or orange) represents ARC-JSD, and the second (lighter blue or orange) represents Contextcite. The legend indicates the color coding: dark blue for ARC-JSD on TyDi QA, orange for Contextcite on TyDi QA, light blue for ARC-JSD on Hotpot QA, light orange for Contextcite on Hotpot QA, very light blue for ARC-JSD on MuSiQue, and very light orange for Contextcite on MuSiQue. For all models and datasets, Contextcite consistently requires more time than ARC-JSD. The most significant difference is observed in the MuSiQue dataset with the Gemma2-9B-IT model, where Contextcite takes approximately 80 seconds per sample, while ARC-JSD takes around 15 seconds. In contrast, for Qwen2-1.5B-IT on TyDi QA, both methods are relatively fast, with ARC-JSD at about 2 seconds and Contextcite at about 5 seconds. The bars are arranged in groups by model, with datasets ordered as TyDi QA, Hotpot QA, MuSiQue within each group, and the chart uses a clean, grid-based layout without additional annotations or emphasis on specific bars.
